art.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quieter Sunday for art news, but there's a good mix today, from a guided tour in Grenoble to a hidden self-portrait in the Sistine Chapel.

Let me start close to home. This afternoon at half past two, the Musée de Grenoble is holding a guided tour of its François Morellet exhibition, open to the public. The title is "Sous la géométrie, la facétie", which promises playfulness beneath the geometry, and that sounds like the right spirit for a Sunday afternoon. If you can get down from Les Adrets, it seems well worth considering. Also in the region, Le Dauphiné Libéré reports that Denise Chochillon's exhibition on the First World War is visible again at Alissas. The piece gives few details, but a local show that touches on history may be worth a look.

Now to the connections between painting and writing, which I know you enjoy. Hyperallergic highlights a new book by James Cahill that begins with David Hockney's portrait of the arts patron Betty Freeman. From that single painting, it tells the story of two friends who shaped the cultural life of Los Angeles in the nineteen-sixties. It sounds like a painting used as a doorway into a richly narrated human story. Hyperallergic also looks at El Museo del Barrio, which is restaging Papo Colo's "Octopus and Others", a show pairing text and image that was first seen four decades ago. It's a rare chance to see how a poet and an artist worked together, on the page and on the wall.

In Paris, the Bibliothèque nationale de France is presenting sixty years of work by the feminist cartoonist Agnès Rosenstiehl, drawing on a donation of more than seven hundred original drawings. Beaux Arts Magazine quotes the line "Mimi Cracra, c'est moi", and the piece suggests a lively, personal body of work that sits somewhere between drawing, satire and the printed page. Beaux Arts also reports that UNESCO is shining a light on Lucia Moholy, a photographer who helped shape the image of the Bauhaus and who worked on heritage preservation. She is a woman long overshadowed, and the story feels like a good corrective to the usual account of modernist design.

And since fiction is never far from your mind, a note outside the visual arts. BBC Radio 4's Front Row broadcast a thirty-minute special from Old Billingsgate in London, announcing the winner of the twenty twenty-six Booker Prize live from the ceremony. The shortlist of six includes novels by Elizabeth Strout and Douglas Stuart, and the judges include Mary Beard and Jarvis Cocker. I won't pretend to tell you the result here, but it may be worth finding the programme.

For painting and its making, there is a striking story from Rome. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that during the cleaning of Michelangelo's Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel, conservators have reportedly found an unprecedented technique and a hidden self-portrait of the artist. The text is only a brief teaser, so details are thin, but for anyone who loves paintings and how they come to be, it's a tantalising discovery. I'd keep an eye out for fuller coverage.

Brussels features twice in the news. At the Villa Empain in Brussels, an exhibition brings the Symbolist painter Léon Spilliaert out of the shadows, looking beyond his deserted landscapes and tormented self-portraits. Beaux Arts calls the setting sumptuous, and the piece sounds like an intriguing introduction to a painter with a strong, haunting presence. Meanwhile, the Petit Palais in Paris presents Brussels around nineteen hundred, with the paintings of James Ensor and the Art Nouveau architecture of Victor Horta. It also takes a critical look at colonial plunder, so painting, architecture and history are all held together in one show.

Across the Channel, The Guardian has plenty. It reports that the thickly palette-knifed Welsh landscapes of Sir Kyffin Williams have been animated and set to music in an immersive show at the National Library of Wales. It's a fresh way of looking at paint, and the rugged Welsh scenery may appeal to you. The Guardian's weekly round-up notes that Turner Contemporary in Margate is hosting a free display by Nicole Eisenman, described as witty and imaginative, running from the fourteenth of November to the eleventh of April. The same dispatch touches on Scottish Roman history and on work by Wolfgang Tillmans and Tracey Emin. And The Guardian reviews "How Do We Find Love?", the Sainsbury Centre in Norwich's winter series on the subject, made up of "The Last Human Kiss" and "Ecstasy and the Aftermath". The critic finds some uplifting works, though feels the theme is handled with a certain obviousness.

Finally, two lighter pieces. The Guardian picks out five beautiful eco buildings around the world, from a bamboo gym in Bali to an earth house in Wiltshire, and including the Children's Village in Tocantins, Brazil. The angle is design and climate rather than art history, but it makes the case that green architecture can be lovely too. And the paper's series on the best phone pictures features Maurice Bakley's photograph from a school eclipse watch party in Arlington, Virginia, taken from a child's-eye view. The title quotes him saying that none of the children had ever seen an eclipse in real life, which is a charming thing to hold in mind.

That's all for today, Yamuna, and I hope the Sunday light is kind to you, whether you spend it with Morellet or with a good book.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Sunday the fifteenth of November, and the last two days have brought a lovely mix of paintings that tell stories, artists who worked with writers, and a few quiet rediscoveries, with one thing happening in Grenoble this very afternoon.

Let me begin close to home. At the Musée de Grenoble, there is a guided tour today of the François Morellet exhibition, at half past two. It's open to the public, and the title is rather wonderful: "Sous la géométrie, la facétie", which you might render as playfulness beneath the geometry. I like that promise. Geometry has a reputation for being severe and a little cold, and here the title suggests that the rules are there to be teased. If your Sunday allows it, it could be a very pleasant way to spend an hour or so, and it's the sort of tour where someone talks you through how to look, which can change an abstract work entirely. A second local note comes from Le Dauphiné Libéré, which reports that Denise Chochillon's exhibition on the First World War at Alissas is visible again. The report gives few details, so I can't tell you much about what's in it, but it's a reminder that local shows about that war keep reappearing, and they're often a good way into history through objects and faces rather than dates.

Now to the theme I suspect will please you most, which is where painting meets writing. The Hyperallergic site has a piece on James Cahill's new book, which takes David Hockney's portrait of the arts patron Betty Freeman as its starting point. From that one painting, Cahill tells the story of two friends who shaped the cultural life of Los Angeles in the nineteen-sixties. It sounds like a book where a single canvas opens onto a whole world: a city, a circle of people, a particular moment. The review describes it as richly narrated, and it's the kind of thing that could work beautifully in a classroom, because it shows a portrait as a door into a life, not just an image to be described. The phrase in the headline, "the secret life of a Beverly Hills housewife", has a novelistic ring to it, as though the sitter has more going on behind the pose than the picture first admits.

Also from Hyperallergic, there's news from New York. El Museo del Barrio is restaging Papo Colo's "Octopus and Others", a show that pairs text and image and was first seen four decades ago. The piece frames it as an artist-poet collaboration, with something almost alchemical in it, and it's a rare chance to see how a poet and an artist worked together, on the page and on the wall. I find that idea appealing: the poem not as a caption to the picture, nor the picture as an illustration of the poem, but the two sparking against each other. If you ever want an example for students of how words and images can share a space as equals, this is a promising one.

And, in the same spirit, Paris. The Bibliothèque nationale de France is presenting sixty years of work by the feminist cartoonist Agnès Rosenstiehl, drawing on a donation of more than seven hundred original drawings. Beaux Arts Magazine quotes her under the headline "Mimi Cracra, c'est moi", which tells you the character and the author are closely entwined. The piece suggests a lively and personal body of work, sitting somewhere between drawing, satire and the printed page. It's a good reminder that a narrator doesn't have to be a prose voice at all; a drawn character can carry a whole sensibility, and here that character seems to carry a woman's long career.

While we're on the subject of fiction, and though it sits outside the visual arts, I should mention that BBC Radio 4's Front Row has a thirty-minute special, broadcast live from Old Billingsgate in London, announcing the winner of the twenty twenty-six Booker Prize. Six novels were shortlisted, including those by Elizabeth Strout and Douglas Stuart, and the judges include Mary Beard and Jarvis Cocker. That's a fascinating panel: a classicist and a songwriter sitting among the novelists' work. I can't tell you the result from what I have in front of me, but the programme will be a pleasant listen if you want to hear the winner announced and the reaction in the room.

Let me turn now to rediscoveries and the making of paintings. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that during the cleaning of Michelangelo's Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel, conservators have reportedly found an unprecedented technique and a hidden self-portrait by the artist. The text I have is only a short teaser, so I can't give you the particulars of what the technique is or where the self-portrait is hiding, and I'd treat the word "reportedly" seriously until more detail appears. But even as a headline it's striking. There's something thrilling about the idea that one of the most looked-at paintings in the world can still hold a secret, and that it takes the slow, patient work of cleaning to bring it out. It has a touch of the detective story about it, which I think suits you.

Another quiet rediscovery is that of Lucia Moholy. UNESCO is highlighting this photographer, who helped shape the image of the Bauhaus and also worked on heritage preservation. Beaux Arts Magazine calls her a little-known pioneer, which is a polite way of saying that history overlooked her. It's a fine story of a woman long overshadowed, and it has clear links to the history of modernist design: when we picture the Bauhaus, we often picture it through photographs, and here is someone whose eye helped make those pictures. It's a nice case of asking who was behind the camera.

Brussels is having something of a moment in the same magazine's pages. At the Villa Empain, an exhibition brings the Symbolist painter Léon Spilliaert out of the shadows, moving beyond the deserted landscapes and tormented self-portraits he is best known for. Those two phrases alone are evocative: empty shores, and a face looking back at you with unease. The article calls the setting sumptuous, and I like the contrast between a grand villa and a painter so drawn to solitude. It's described as an intriguing introduction, so if his name is new to you, or only half-familiar, this might be a good place to start.

And in Paris, the Petit Palais presents Brussels around nineteen hundred, with the paintings of James Ensor and the Art Nouveau architecture of Victor Horta. What I find interesting is that the show doesn't look away from the darker side of the story: it addresses colonial plunder, so the creative ferment of the city is shown alongside the history that helped pay for it. That combination of painting, architecture and a frank account of the past is the sort of thing that teaches history more honestly than a tidy timeline. Taken together with Spilliaert, it makes for a rich picture of Belgian art at the turn of the century, from the haunted to the exuberant.

Across the Channel, The Guardian has several pieces. The most visually exciting is about Sir Kyffin Williams, whose thickly palette-knifed Welsh landscapes have been animated and set to music in an immersive show at the National Library of Wales. Kyffin Williams painted in heavy, sculpted strokes, and the idea of those surfaces moving, with music beneath them, is a fresh way of experiencing painting. I'd be curious whether it adds to the paint or competes with it, but the Welsh landscapes alone may appeal to you, and the combination of land, paint and sound is almost a poem in itself.

The Guardian's weekly roundup, headed "the week in art", notes that from the fourteenth of November until the eleventh of April, Turner Contemporary in Margate hosts a free display by Nicole Eisenman, which it describes as witty and imaginative. The same column ranges over Scottish Roman history and work by Wolfgang Tillmans and Tracey Emin, so it's a handy overview if you like a broad sweep of what's on in Britain.

There is also a review of the Sainsbury Centre in Norwich's winter series on love, titled "How Do We Find Love?", made up of two shows, The Last Human Kiss and Ecstasy and the Aftermath. The critic finds some uplifting works, from lipsmacking kisses through to tears of despair, though the theme is handled with a certain obviousness. I rather enjoy that honest note: love is, after all, the oldest subject in literature, and it's hard to say something new about it. It might be a nice prompt for a class discussion about why the great themes so often feel predictable in the wrong hands and so alive in the right ones.

Last, two pieces on how we see the world around us. The Guardian has a feature called "It's an architect's dream", on five beautiful eco buildings around the world, from a bamboo gym in Bali to an earth house in Wiltshire. The Children's Village in Tocantins, Brazil, is among them. The angle is design and climate rather than art history, but the point is a gentle one, that green building can also be lovely to look at. And the paper's series on the best phone pictures features Maurice Bakley's photograph from a school eclipse watch party in Arlington, Virginia, taken from a child's-eye view. The title quotes a remark that none of the children had ever seen an eclipse in real life, which is a lovely line, and the story behind the photo is charming and human.

That's all for this morning, Yamuna. I hope the geometry at the Musée de Grenoble proves as playful as its title promises.

literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. The past two days have been dominated by one story, a surprising Booker Prize, with a few lovely things about sentences, new novels and shared reading alongside it.

Let me begin with the prize. M John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker for fiction with The End of Everything, at the age of eighty-one. NPR notes that he is the first science fiction author ever to take the prize, a real milestone for a genre that has so often been kept at the margins. The Guardian's editorial calls the win a new frontier for science fiction, and it places the novel within the longer history and development of the genre, so it may be a good place to start if you want context before the book itself.

What I enjoyed most is hearing Harrison speak, because the interviews are wonderfully characterful. In The i Paper, he says, and I rather love this, "I'm going to die soon. I can do what I like." It is candid and unsentimental, and it makes late recognition sound less like a crown than a kind of liberation. The Irish Times gives a warmer, more private picture. There he describes lying awake most of the night, thinking, "This is extraordinary." The two together make a nice pair: the dry humour by day and the astonishment in the small hours.

Then there is the interview in The Times of India, which is the one I would point you towards as a teacher. Harrison says, "Fiction is a vibe. You're like TS Eliot. Your job is to give people a feeling of something." Whatever one makes of the word vibe, the claim underneath is a serious one: that a novelist works like a poet, through atmosphere and feeling rather than through plot alone. That might make a good provocation for a première class, set beside a few lines of Eliot, to ask whether they agree that fiction is about the feeling first.

Not everyone is delighted, though. bdnews24 carries an opinion piece from a writer who has loved Harrison's work for years, and who is defending him after what it describes as a divided reaction. Many people, it says, disliked the choice. It reads as a personal appreciation rather than news, so it offers more of the case for the fiction than the case against. Frontline Magazine takes a gentler angle, looking at the win as late-career recognition for a distinctive writer, and it may be a useful way in if you have not read him. The Guardian also has a piece headed "The End of Everything is the beginning of something great", which sounds like a warm review, although I have only the headline, so I cannot tell you its argument. The Booker is also turning up elsewhere: The Borderlens reports on the Shillong Literary Fest, in north-east India, which brings Khasi heritage and Booker laureates together in a celebration of storytelling. It is a nice reminder of local tradition and oral history sitting beside international prize-winners, and it fits your interest in fiction that carries history.

Moving on from the Booker, there is a new novel I think you may like. The New York Times reviews Stations by Louise Kennedy, published today. It follows a young Irishwoman in London who tests the limits of commitment. The review presents it as a character-driven book, and given how much you value a strong central voice, it seems worth keeping an eye on.

If you want to savour language for its own sake, The Paris Review has its November Bookmarks, a selection of passages that people have underlined in new releases. This month's is titled "A Single Woman in a Dust-Proof Room". I have only the framing and not the passages themselves, but a collection of striking sentences chosen by readers is a pleasant thing to dip into with a cup of tea, and some of them might be good for a short close-reading exercise.

For something to read next, Literary Hub's weekly roundup features Maris Kreizman recommending ten debut novels from 2026 that readers may have missed. The summary is brief, so the list itself is the draw, and debuts are often where you find the freshest narrators. The same roundup has an interview with Olivia Waite, a former New York Times romance columnist, about being fired, if that interests you.

And two more from Literary Hub, one ambitious and one playful. The ambitious one is an invitation: Equator magazine is running a reading group in 2027 on Roberto Bolaño's 2666. It follows a summer edition devoted to Mike Davis's Late Victorian Holocausts. If 2666 has been sitting on your shelf, unread, for too long, then a year with company might be the push it needs. The playful one is a craft piece arguing that following the Buffalo Bills, even through the losses, can teach a writer something about writing. It comes with an excerpt about an editor-in-chief lost among identical office cubicles. The text I have is short, but the tone sounds fun, and the excerpt promises some good scene-setting.

So, a prize for a late-blooming writer, a few sentences worth underlining, and perhaps a big book to tackle next year. I hope your Sunday has a good chair and a good page in it.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. The literary world has been talking about one thing this weekend, the Booker Prize, so we begin there, then turn to a new novel, some lovely sentences, a festival in north-east India, and a few things for your reading pile.

The news is that M. John Harrison has won the twenty twenty-six Booker Prize for fiction, with a novel called The End of Everything. He is eighty-one. NPR points out that he is the first science fiction author ever to win the prize, which is a real milestone for a genre that has so often been kept at the margins of literary prizegiving. The Guardian has devoted an editorial to the win, calling it a new frontier for science fiction, and it places the novel within the longer history and development of the genre. Its argument is that this is not only a victory for one writer but a moment when the borders between kinds of fiction look a little less fixed than they did.

What I find most appealing in the coverage is how much of it comes in the writer's own voice, because Harrison seems to be a delight to interview. The i Paper has him saying, quite cheerfully, "I'm going to die soon. I can do what I like." There is something wonderfully liberating in that. He is eighty-one, he has just won one of the most celebrated prizes in English-language writing, and his response is not pomp but a kind of freedom. It is a candid, characterful remark, and it gives the whole story a lovely edge of mischief.

The Irish Times caught him in a gentler mood. There, he describes lying awake for much of the night, thinking, "This is extraordinary." That is a very human detail. After a long career, the news has not settled into comfortable acceptance; it has kept him awake with wonder. Put the two interviews side by side and you get a writer who is wry about mortality and still astonished by good fortune. Neither seems at all like the usual script for prize winners, and both are well worth reading for the voice alone.

The interview I would single out for you, though, is the one in The Times of India. Asked about his craft, Harrison reportedly said, "Fiction is a vibe. You're like T. S. Eliot. Your job is to give people a feeling of something." I love that, partly for the casual word "vibe" sitting next to a name like Eliot, and partly because it says something true about how certain kinds of writing work. Not every novel needs to explain itself or resolve itself; some succeed by leaving an atmosphere, a feeling, in the reader. If you teach poetry alongside prose, as you do, that remark might make a good starting point for a conversation with your première students about what they actually feel when they read, and whether they can say why. It is a bold thing for a novelist to claim kinship with Eliot, but I suspect a few of your students would enjoy arguing about it.

Not everyone is celebrating, mind you. A piece on bdnews24 acknowledges that many people disliked this year's winner, and then offers a personal defence from a writer who has loved Harrison's work for years. It is an opinion piece, more an appreciation than a news report, but it is a useful reminder that a Booker win rarely arrives without argument. A divided reaction can be the sign of a book doing something unusual. I will not claim to know the details of the quarrel, since the coverage I have is brief, but if you enjoy seeing how a prize provokes readers into defending what they love, that essay is the one to try.

Frontline Magazine also looks at the win, under the heading "A Booker Prize at eighty-one", and concentrates on the late-career side of the story. There is something heartening in the recognition of a distinctive writer so far into a working life. Frontline's piece may be a good entry point if you are new to his fiction and want to know where to begin. And The Guardian has a separate piece headlined "The End of Everything is the beginning of something great". I only have the headline, so I cannot tell you what it argues, but the title suggests a warm and generous review. If you would like to know what the book is actually like on the page, that would be my first stop.

Now, away from the Booker and towards something newly out. The New York Times reviews Louise Kennedy's novel Stations, which is published today. It follows a young Irishwoman in London who tests the limits of commitment. The review presents it as a character-driven novel, and that, I think, is why it might suit you. A young woman far from home, deciding how much of herself she can promise to people and places, is the kind of premise that lives or dies on voice and on the small details of a person's behaviour. If the review is right, it is a book to step into rather than study from outside.

For something to savour in small doses, The Paris Review has published its November Bookmarks, under the title "A Single Woman in a Dust-Proof Room". These are passages that the magazine's people have underlined in new releases, so you get a handful of striking sentences without having to commit to whole books. I find this a lovely way to read, a bit like walking round a gallery and stopping at the pictures that catch your eye. If you collect passages for class, or simply for pleasure, it is a gentle way to spend a quiet Sunday morning, perhaps with a coffee after the market.

From the Paris Review we go a long way east, to the Shillong Literary Fest, which The Borderlens reports on. The festival brings together Khasi heritage and Booker laureates, in what the report describes as a celebration of the power of stories. I like the pairing. On one side you have local tradition and oral history, stories carried by communities long before they were printed; on the other, international prize-winners, writers who have been through the machinery of literary fame. Seeing them share a stage says something about how stories travel, and how the oldest forms of telling and the most modern still belong to the same family. It also fits your fondness for fiction that teaches history, since oral traditions are often where a place keeps its memory. I have only the broad outline of the report, but it is a cheerful piece, and a good one for anyone who likes literary festivals.

Now a few things for your reading life. Literary Hub reports that the magazine Equator is running a book club in twenty twenty-seven devoted to Roberto Bolaño's 2666. It follows a summer edition on Mike Davis's Late Victorian Holocausts. The idea is plainly to help readers who have put the novel off for too long finally to tackle it, with company. Whether or not you sign up, the invitation has a certain appeal. Some books are easier to begin when you know others are reading alongside you, and a long, demanding novel can feel more like a shared expedition than a solitary slog. If it has been sitting on your shelf, a whole year is a generous amount of time to approach it.

Literary Hub's weekly roundup, covering the ninth to the thirteenth of November, includes a list from Maris Kreizman of ten debut novels from this year that readers may have missed. For someone who enjoys discovering new voices, that is a good list to browse, and a handy way of catching up on first novels that did not get much attention. The same roundup has an interview, by Zachary Fletcher, with Olivia Waite, the former New York Times romance columnist, about being fired. It is more about the book-reviewing world than about writing itself, so I mention it only briefly, in case it interests you.

Finally, Literary Hub's daily newsletter from the thirteenth has a playful craft piece arguing that following the Buffalo Bills, even through the losses, can teach a writer something about writing. I know nothing about the details of the argument, and I suspect sport is not your natural territory, but there is something rather charming about the idea that loyalty through disappointment is a kind of education in storytelling. Alongside it is an excerpt about an editor-in-chief lost among identical office cubicles. The text I have is short, but the tone is light and the setting sounds wonderfully absurd, and the situation itself promises some good scene-setting. A small treat, perhaps, for a lunch break.

So, to gather it together. The big story is Harrison, a writer at eighty-one who is both amused and astonished by his own success, and who thinks that fiction's job is to give people a feeling. Around him there is a new novel to try, a handful of lovely sentences to collect, a festival where old stories meet new ones, and the beginnings of a plan for Bolaño. If you read only one thing today, I would suggest the Times of India interview, since it has the line about Eliot, or the Irish Times for the sleepless-night warmth. And if you would rather have a novel than an interview, Louise Kennedy's Stations is out this very day.

That is the literature briefing for this Sunday, Yamuna; may your cup be hot and your next sentence be a good one.

around.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. There is a gentle mix of documentaries, music and exhibitions around you this week, with a few things still to catch today and a good deal to plan for the weeks ahead.

Let me begin with today, and with your own village. This afternoon, the fifteenth of November, from five until half past seven in the evening, the Salle Pelloux-Prayer in Les Adrets hosts a screening called Tero Loko, cultiver l'accueil, part of the Mois du Doc. The listing says very little about the film itself, but a documentary evening a few steps from home is a rare thing, so it seemed worth putting first. Also ending today is the second contemporary art fair at the Maison des Arts in Montbonnot-Saint-Martin. It has been running since the thirteenth, so if painting and visual art tempt you, this is the last chance.

Yesterday, the fourteenth, was a busy day in the valley, and it shows how lively the Mois du Doc has become. In Pontcharra, from half past five until seven, there was a screening of the documentary Aurores Boréales. Then in Froges, at the Église Sainte-Thérèse, a concert of Nordic chants ran from six until half past seven. Those two make a rather lovely pair, with the northern lights on screen and northern voices in a church, though I suspect that was luck rather than design. If either one passed you by, keep an eye out for similar evenings, as the Mois du Doc is still under way.

Two other events yesterday had a different flavour. In Allevard, at La Pléiade, there was a second-hand ski swap from nine until five. It is aimed at skiers, but it has all the spirit of a good flea market, with people hunting for a bargain. And in Le Cheylas, in the evening, Serge Caillet gave a talk on Monsieur Philippe de Lyon. The listing says little more, but the name suggests a figure from Lyon's past, which might interest you if you like history told through people.

Now to things that give you more time. In the Chartreuse hills, at Le Sappey-en-Chartreuse, a free exhibition called Hier, au temps futur opened on the thirteenth of November and runs until the thirtieth of January. That is a long run, and it could make a quiet winter outing, perhaps with a walk on either side. In Grenoble itself, there is a free display on the military high-mountain group, the Groupe Militaire de Haute Montagne, open until the thirty-first of December. The details are thin, but it is a piece of local mountain history and it stays open for the rest of the year. Also in Grenoble, the local paper Le Journal des Savoie... or rather, the site jds.fr, reports on an immersive light-and-sound show built around water, coming to a museum in the city. No dates were given in the piece, so it is worth watching for them, but the idea of water, light and sound together sounds quite beautiful.

December is where the stage calendar starts to fill, and most of it centres on the MC2 in Grenoble. The first date is the third of December, when there is an open studio session of RODA with Aina Alegre. Details are sparse, but an open studio is a chance to see work close up, before it is polished. Then, from the ninth to the eleventh of December, the MC2 stages Article 353 du code pénal, by Tanguy Viel and Emmanuel Noblet. This one may especially appeal to you, because it takes Viel's literary text and brings it to the stage, so you can hear a writer's narration and characters carried by actors. Then on the tenth of December comes the second of three encounter sessions called Le monde en musiques. The description is brief, but it is a musical evening at the same venue, so you could combine it with the play if you fancied a couple of nights in town.

On the cinema side, which I know is not your main interest, the Dolce Cinema festival is celebrating its twentieth edition, in Grenoble and elsewhere in Isère. The report I have gives no dates, but twenty years is a good run for a local festival, so it is a pleasant thing to know about.

And finally, two notes from the mountains. Grenoble Mag reports that the first snow has fallen on the summits of Isère, and it urges caution before the resorts open. That is a seasonal sign from the ridges above you, so if you are planning a walk in Belledonne, keep it in mind. And France 3 Alpes tells a rather charming story about Béal, a company founded in nineteen fifty and based in Isère, which has become the world leader in climbing and rescue ropes. Its success rests on a very absorbent dynamic rope, and the recipe is still kept secret. It is not culture exactly, but it is a good tale of local craft and invention, and one that might even interest your pupils.

That is all for today, Yamuna. I hope you find a quiet moment for the film in Les Adrets this afternoon.
around.long:

It's Sunday the fifteenth of November, and this morning's round-up of what's happening around you opens with a documentary in your own village, then takes in the weekend that has just passed, some long-running exhibitions, a handful of December dates at the MC2, and a little news from the mountains.

It belongs to the Mois du Doc, the month of documentary film that is running through the Grésivaudan this November. The listing says very little about the film itself, so I can't tell you what it's about beyond the title. But the title is intriguing, and an event in your own village, at the end of a Sunday, with no travelling involved, is hard to argue with. If you fancy a gentle evening, it may be the easiest outing of the week.

Also today, and it ends today, is the second edition of the Salon d'art contemporain at the Maison des Arts in Montbonnot-Saint-Martin. It has been running since Friday the thirteenth, so this is the last day. I don't have details of the artists or what's being shown, only that it's a contemporary art fair. But given how much you enjoy the conversation between painting and the written word, it might be worth a short drive down the valley if you have an hour to spare before the afternoon documentary. If you can't make it, at least you know it exists, and that it's now in its second year, which suggests there may be a third.

Now the Mois du Doc has a second entry nearby, though this one was yesterday. On Saturday the fourteenth, from half past five until seven in the evening, Pontcharra screened the documentary Aurores Boréales, the northern lights. The listing gives no more than that. I mention it partly in case you went, and partly because it shows how wide the Mois du Doc programme is across the valley. If it goes on into the coming weeks, it may be worth keeping an eye on what the Grésivaudan listings offer next, since you clearly have two or three of these within a short drive.

Also yesterday evening, from six until half past seven, there was a concert of Nordic chants at the Église Sainte-Thérèse in Froges. I like the pairing, in fact: northern lights in Pontcharra, Nordic voices in Froges, all on the same Saturday evening. If you managed to hear it, I hope it was lovely. A concert of voices in a village church, in mid-November with the evenings drawing in, is exactly the sort of local music that suits the season. I have no programme details, so I can't say which chants were sung, but the setting alone gives a sense of the atmosphere.

Two other things happened in the valley yesterday, both rather different in character. In Allevard, at La Pléiade, there was a second-hand ski swap, a bourse aux skis, from nine in the morning until five in the afternoon. It has the spirit of a flea market, rummaging and bargain-hunting and chatting to the people on the other side of the table, though it is naturally aimed at skiers rather than at books or paintings. Whether or not you ski, these swaps tend to be a sign that the season is about to begin, and that brings me to the snow, which I'll come back to in a moment.

And at Le Cheylas, from a quarter past seven until ten in the evening, there was a talk by Serge Caillet on Monsieur Philippe de Lyon. The listing says little else, but the name suggests a figure from Lyon, and a long evening devoted to a single historical personality sounds like the kind of thing that could teach a good deal. I can't tell you more than that, since I only have the title and the speaker, but I thought you might be curious about the subject, particularly as you like history told through people.

So that's the weekend. Now for things that are still to come, and let's start with the exhibitions that give you time. The first is a free exhibition called Hier, au temps futur, which translates roughly as Yesterday, in the future tense. It opened on the thirteenth of November and runs until the thirtieth of January, at Le Sappey-en-Chartreuse. I know no more than the title and the dates, but the length of the run is the useful part. Nearly three months in the Chartreuse hills means you can choose a quiet winter day, perhaps a bright one after snow, and combine it with a walk or a lunch. It's free, which removes any pressure about whether it will be worth it. And I rather like the title, which sounds like something a novelist might have chosen.

The second long-running display is in Grenoble, and it's about the Groupe militaire de haute montagne, the military high-mountain group. It's free, and it runs until the thirty-first of December, having opened back in February. The details I have are thin, so I can't describe what's on show. But it's a piece of local mountain history, and you have the rest of the year to see it. With the snow arriving, there's a certain appeal to looking at how people trained to work in this terrain, in the city that sits right beneath it.

Then there's something with no dates attached, so I'll be honest about that. The Journal des Savoie, or jds.fr, reports on an immersive light and sound show built around water, coming to a museum in Grenoble. It's called Lumières au musée. I don't have the dates, nor which museum, so it's one to check in the local listings before you plan anything. But an immersive evening in a museum, with water as its subject, sounds like it could be visually striking, and you may find the combination of light, sound and architecture rewarding.

Let me turn to December, because the MC2 in Grenoble has a cluster of dates, and a couple of them seem well suited to you.

The first is on the third of December: an open studio session of RODA with Aina Alegre. An open studio is when an artist lets the public in to see work in progress rather than a finished show, and I can't tell you more than that, because the listing doesn't say what form it will take. But I mention it because you enjoy documentaries about dance, and the open-studio format lets you see how a piece is made, which is often just as interesting as the performance itself.

Then, from the ninth to the eleventh of December, the MC2 stages Article 353 du code pénal, by Tanguy Viel and Emmanuel Noblet. This is a literary text brought to the stage, and I think that's the point that matters for you. Viel is a novelist, and the evening takes his written work into performance. For someone who loves narrators and the sound of a voice carrying a story, I'd say it deserves a look. Three evenings give you some flexibility, and since it's a text you could read first, you might even want to pick up the book beforehand and then see what the stage does with it. That's a suggestion, of course, not something I can promise is wise, since I know nothing of the staging itself.

And on the tenth of December, also at the MC2, there's the second of three sessions called Le monde en musiques, a series of encounters around world music. The description is brief, and I don't know who's taking part, but if you like classical music and musical documentaries, the idea of an evening devoted to listening and talking might appeal. It overlaps with Article 353, so you'd need to choose between the two on that particular night, or else go to the play on the ninth or eleventh and the music on the tenth. That would make for a rather rich week at the MC2.

One more cultural note, this time about cinema, though I'll keep it short since I know it's a lower priority for you. The Dolce Cinema festival is celebrating its twentieth edition, held in Grenoble and in other places across Isère, according to the site mesinfos. The text is short and gives me no dates or programme. But twenty years is a long time for a local festival to survive, and it's a pleasant thing to hear about. If it turns out to include something in your corner of the valley, you'll want to know, so it may be worth a quick look at its programme.

Finally, two items from the mountains. The first is seasonal. Grenoble Mag reports that the first snow has fallen on the summits of Isère, and that people are being urged to be careful before the ski resorts open. I only have the headline, so I can't give you the details of conditions or opening dates. But it's a useful reminder, with Belledonne above you, that the season is turning. If you're planning a walk in the high country, the message seems to be to be prudent, since early snow can make familiar paths feel quite different. Down in the valley, the ski swap at Allevard yesterday fits the picture rather nicely.

The second is a good local story, even if it isn't culture. France 3 Alpes reports on Béal, the Isère company founded in 1950 that has become the world leader in ropes for climbing and rescue. The key is its dynamic rope, which absorbs shocks extremely well, and which the company keeps a closely guarded secret in terms of how it's made. One person quoted in the piece calls the business "hyper confidentiel", very confidential. I like it as a story about craft and invention, about a regional firm quietly doing something very well for seventy-odd years, and about the secret recipe that sits behind it. It's rather like a small novel in itself, with a hidden formula at the centre and the mountains behind.

So, to gather it up: the documentary this afternoon in Les Adrets is the one to catch, with the art fair at Montbonnot ending today for anyone who can fit it in. The exhibitions at Le Sappey and in Grenoble give you plenty of time, and December at the MC2 looks full of promise, especially if you're tempted by Viel's text on stage.

I hope your Sunday is a gentle one, Yamuna, and that the first snow on Belledonne is as lovely to look at as it sounds.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's been a Hamlet-heavy couple of days in the theatre pages, with a few good hooks for your Twelfth Night, Rivals and Milk Wood classes, and Margaret Atwood turning up in rather unexpected places.

Let me begin with Hamlet, since most of the news is about it. A production called Hamlet Hail to the Thief has opened at the Barbican in London, and the reviews arrived together. Liam O'Dell calls it a dark and noisy spectacle in which Radiohead and Shakespeare collide. The Line of Best Fit is more playful, with a headline that cheers the show as a Shakespeare reboot. South London reviews it too, as does The Stage, which looks at it as a Hamlet production at the Barbican Theatre. The Evening Standard has a feature on how Shakespeare and Radiohead came together to make the piece, and it explores the link between the play and contemporary music. Some of these pieces were supplied to me as headlines only, so I can't tell you how closely the staging follows the text, or what it cuts. But for a teacher, the useful point is the pairing itself. Hamlet is on the 2027 programme, and a production that sets the play against a modern band's music is a ready-made way into a conversation about adaptation. You could ask your students what a soundtrack adds to a soliloquy, and what it might drown out. Reading O'Dell's description of noise and darkness alongside the Standard's feature would give you two quite different angles on the same show.

There is a second modern take on the play, this time from New York or at least from a company announcing it through BroadwayWorld. COPE Productions will present See What I See, a sapphic reimagining of Hamlet, at a venue called Madame X. The announcement gives no dates, so it's one to watch rather than plan around. Still, between the Barbican and this, you have two very different recent responses to the same set text, which could make a neat comparison for première students thinking about how far a play can be bent before it breaks.

Moving to the other works on the 2027 list, there's some cheerful news from Turkey. Kocaeli Theatres has premiered Twelfth Night in its Grand Hall, and the Foro3D report, dated the thirteenth of November, says the house was full. It's a short piece, but I like it, because it's a reminder that a play written for Elizabethan audiences still fills a hall on the other side of Europe. If you want to show students that Twelfth Night is a living script rather than an exam text, a line like that makes a nice opening.

Then there's a gift for The Rivals. Mathrubhumi English ran its Word of the Day on the fourteenth of November, and the word was malapropism, meaning the misuse of a word for one that sounds similar. The term comes from Sheridan's Mrs Malaprop, so you can start a lesson with the word itself, ask students to guess where it comes from, and let them discover that a character has given her name to a whole habit of speech. It's a lovely example of a fictional figure who has outlived her play.

On Under Milk Wood, there's an echo rather than a production. The Italian musician Vinicio Capossela has premiered a piece called Ordine e pulizia, at a second preview of something called Milk Wood Bar. The report on Foro3D is thin, so I can't say how directly it draws on Dylan Thomas, but the name suggests a nod to the play. If you know Capossela's work, it might be worth keeping an eye on, since his music has a very theatrical, storytelling quality. For a class on Thomas's musical, almost sung prose, it's a small reminder that the play keeps inspiring artists beyond Britain.

Now to the oral themes, and Margaret Atwood, who is on the list through The Handmaid's Tale. Britannica has an explainer asking how Atwood reinterpreted the historical settler Susanna Moodie in The Journals of Susanna Moodie. Only the question was supplied, not the answer, but it's a promising topic for students who like the way fiction can rework a real person's life. It connects nicely with your interest in novels that teach history, and it could give oral candidates a way of thinking about how Atwood treats the past in The Handmaid's Tale as well.

Atwood has also written an opinion piece for the Toronto Star, headlined "Eh, is for Canadian arts and culture". I only have the headline, so I can't tell you what she argues, but the title suggests something affectionate and a bit wry. And she is in the news for a rather different reason. CBC reports that she has joined birders on Pelee Island who are objecting to a proposed telecommunications tower, said to be six hundred feet tall. Again it's the headlines that were supplied, so details are limited, but it's a pleasant story about a writer using her name for something she cares about, and a reminder that Atwood is a keen bird lover.

Two more items, both for browsing. The BBC has a piece on how Kent may have inspired Orwell's Animal Farm. Animal Farm isn't on your lists, though Orwell is there through Nineteen Eighty-Four, and I've only seen the headline. But it fits your love of stories rooted in real places. And Book Riot has published its list of the best fiction of the century so far. I only have the title, so I can't judge the choices, but it may turn up some recent novels for your own shelf, or for the library at school.

That's your corner for today, Yamuna. Enjoy the Sunday, and perhaps a little Mrs Malaprop with your coffee.
bfi.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a rather Hamlet-heavy couple of days in the BFI world, with a few pleasant detours into Sheridan, Atwood and Orwell along the way.

Let me begin with the big cluster, because it's hard to miss. A production called Hamlet Hail to the Thief is running at the Barbican in London, and no fewer than five outlets have written about it. It brings Shakespeare's Hamlet together with the music of Radiohead. Since Hamlet is on the session 2027 list, this is useful material for you, even if none of your pupils will be popping over to the Barbican this term.

Let me say what each piece offers. The headlines are more revealing than you might expect. Liam O'Dell's review calls it a "dark and noisy spectacle", and describes Radiohead and Shakespeare as colliding. That's a vivid phrase, and it tells you something about the experience of the evening: loud, bruising, not especially polite to the text. The Line of Best Fit goes for the headline "Hail to the Shakespeare reboot!", which suggests a more celebratory reading, and describes the production as a reworking of the play. I should be honest that for that one I only have the headline, so I can't tell you what the reviewer actually admired or disliked. The Stage and southlondon.co.uk have each reviewed it too, and both are described as useful for thinking about how a modern staging treats the text. The summaries don't give me their verdicts, so I won't invent any.

The fifth piece is different in kind. The London Evening Standard has a feature on how Shakespeare and Radiohead came together to create what it calls a theatrical masterpiece. That's a feature rather than a review, so it may tell you more about how the idea came about, and why those two worlds were put side by side. It's the one I would read first if you want an angle on adaptation.

Here is how I might use the cluster in class. Five different outlets, five different registers: a specialist theatre publication, a local London site, a music-and-culture site, a big city newspaper, and an independent reviewer. That is almost a ready-made comparison exercise. Give première pupils two of the headlines and ask them to predict the tone of each review before reading. "Dark and noisy spectacle" and "Hail to the Shakespeare reboot" make a nice pair, because one sounds like a warning and the other like a cheer, and yet they may be describing the same evening. It's a tidy way into a discussion about how critics frame an adaptation, and about the vocabulary of evaluation, which pupils so often reduce to "good" and "bad". With seconde you could simply ask a gentler question: if you were putting a famous play together with a rock band's music, what would you keep and what would you cut?

There is a further Hamlet item, and it comes from a very different corner. BroadwayWorld reports that COPE Productions will present See What I See, described as a Sapphic reimagining of Hamlet, at Madame X. The announcement gives no dates, so there's nothing to plan around, but it adds a second contemporary reworking to the pile. Set beside the Barbican production, it makes a good point for pupils: Hamlet is a play that keeps being taken apart and rebuilt by people with quite different concerns. One production reaches for a band, the other for a different lens on the characters and their relationships. That's a useful reminder for the written paper, where a pupil who can say that a text invites reinterpretation is already halfway to a decent argument about why it lasts.

Now to the other session 2027 plays, beginning with a cheering little piece of news. Foro3D reports, on the thirteenth of November, that Kocaeli Theatres has premiered Twelfth Night in its Grand Hall, to a full house. The report is brief and I can't tell you anything about the staging, but the simple fact is lovely: a set text from your list, performed in a theatre in Kocaeli, with every seat taken. If you like to remind pupils that these plays are not just exam material but living things that audiences turn up for in cities all over the world, this is a small, true example. It's good news, which I know you appreciate, and it needs no further decoration.

On the same theme of the programme reaching out into the wider world, there is a Word of the Day entry from Mathrubhumi English, dated the fourteenth of November, on the word "malapropism". For anyone who needs the definition, it's the misuse of a word for another that sounds similar. The entry is a handy hook for Sheridan's The Rivals, because Mrs Malaprop is the character who gives the term its name. I like this one because it turns an everyday dictionary entry into a doorway back into the play. You could open a lesson by reading out the definition without saying where it comes from, then ask pupils to guess which character on the programme the word is named after. It also gives a pleasing reversal: a character becomes a word, a fictional figure whose habits have outlived the play and entered common English. That's a nice thing for pupils to notice about the power of a strongly drawn character, which is surely a theme dear to you.

Another Italian-flavoured item comes from Foro3D as well. Vinicio Capossela has premiered a new piece called Ordine e pulizia, at the second preview of something called Milk Wood Bar. The title of the venture echoes Dylan Thomas's Under Milk Wood, which is on the session 2027 list. The text I have is thin, so I can't describe the music or the show itself. What I can say is that the name alone suggests a musician somewhere in Italy has had Thomas's play in his head, which is rather charming. If you teach Under Milk Wood, it could be a small curiosity to share: the play's title, with its sense of a place and its voices, has travelled far enough to name a bar, or at least a performance project. I would treat it as a talking point, not as a resource, until there is more to go on.

Let me turn now to the oral themes, where Margaret Atwood has been busy, or at least much written about. Four items this time.

The most useful for class is from Britannica, an explainer asking how Atwood reinterpreted Susanna Moodie in The Journals of Susanna Moodie. Moodie is described as a historical settler, and the piece looks at what Atwood did with her. I only have the question, not the answer, so I can't summarise the argument. But the question itself is a good one for pupils who study The Handmaid's Tale for the oral. It shows Atwood as a writer who goes back to real historical figures and reimagines them, which connects history and fiction in the way you value. You could ask older pupils: what does it mean for a novelist or poet to take a real person and give them a new voice? What is gained, and what might be lost? That question works for Atwood, and it could just as easily be turned back on Browning's dramatic monologues next year, which are all about speaking in the voice of someone else.

Then there is an opinion piece by Atwood herself in the Toronto Star, on Canadian arts and culture, under a headline playing on the Canadian "eh". I only have the headline, so I can't tell you what she argues. I mention it mainly so you know it exists, in case you want to see Atwood writing in her own voice rather than through fiction.

And then two CBC stories on the same subject. They report that Atwood is joining other bird lovers in pushing back against a proposed telecommunications tower on Pelee Island. One of the headlines gives the height of the tower: six hundred feet. Both pieces are only headlines for me, so I can't tell you where the dispute stands. But as a local nature story with a famous name attached, it's a gentle, human item, a writer showing up for something she loves. It's the sort of thing that humanises an author who, for pupils, may be only a name on a book jacket.

There is a related literary-history item too, which suits your taste for novels that connect to real places. The BBC has a piece on how Kent may have inspired Orwell's Animal Farm. Sadly I only have the headline, so I can't tell you which places or which details the piece draws on. Still, it's a promising idea. Orwell is on the oral list through 1984, and anything that grounds his work in a real landscape may help pupils see that his fiction came from somewhere, rather than arriving fully formed as political allegory. If the full article turns out to be good, it could be a nice bridge to a lesson on how setting shapes a writer's imagination.

Last, a gentle suggestion for your own reading, or perhaps for the bookshelf at school. Book Riot has a list of the best fiction books of the century so far. I only have the title, so I cannot say what is on it, and I wouldn't want to guess. But a list like that can be a pleasant source of recent novels, and if there are titles you don't know, it may suggest wider reading for pupils who finish the set works and ask what to try next. Prophet Song, on your oral list, is a recent novel of exactly that type, so you may find some company for it.

To pull the threads together: the strongest classroom material today is the Hamlet cluster, especially if you set the reviews against each other, with the Evening Standard feature for the background on how the idea came about. The Malaprop hook is the quickest win, since it needs no preparation at all. And the Britannica question on Atwood and Moodie is the most thought-provoking for older pupils, even though it is only a question for now.

A caution, too. Several of these items reached me as headlines only, so it would be worth opening the full pieces yourself before building anything around them. Those are the Britannica explainer, the Toronto Star column, the two CBC stories, the BBC piece on Kent and Orwell, the Book Riot list and the Line of Best Fit review.

That's the corner for today, Yamuna, and I hope you find a spare moment this weekend to enjoy a little Shakespeare, loud or otherwise.

good.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It has been a gentle couple of days for good news, with a great deal of it coming from the world of words and stories, so let us begin there.

The big literary moment is that M. John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize for fiction with The End of Everything. NPR reports that he is the first science fiction author ever to take the prize, which is a real milestone for a genre so often kept at the margins. The Guardian, in an editorial, calls it a new frontier for science fiction, and places the novel within the longer history and development of the genre, so it is a good place to start if you want to understand why this matters.

What I enjoyed most, though, is how Harrison himself has reacted. He is eighty-one, and he has been giving wonderfully candid interviews. In The i Paper, his headline line is that he is going to die soon, and so he can do what he likes. It is a characterful thing to say, funny and a little defiant, and it makes late recognition sound less like a crown and more like a licence. The Irish Times caught a softer side. He told them he is awake most of the night thinking, "This is extraordinary." Between the two you get a rather lovely portrait of a writer who has been at it for decades and is still astonished.

Staying with stories, The Borderlens reports on the Shillong Literary Fest, in north-east India, which brings together Khasi heritage and Booker laureates in a celebration of storytelling. I like the pairing of local tradition and oral history with international prize-winners, as though the two were simply part of the same long conversation.

Now to paintings and to words in the making. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that during the cleaning of Michelangelo's Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel, conservators have reportedly found an unprecedented technique and a hidden self-portrait of the artist. The piece is only a short teaser so far, so details are thin, but it is a striking thought that a fresco so famous can still be hiding something of its maker.

A similar pleasure of seeing how a famous work was put together comes from Good News Network. A handwritten draft of Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I Have a Dream" speech, written on the morning of the march to the Lincoln Memorial, has resurfaced after six decades, emerging from a desk drawer. It is heavily revised, which shows just how carefully he worked on the words. For a teacher of literature, I imagine that is a gift: a rare chance to watch a great text being made, crossings-out and all. It might even be something to put in front of a class.

Next, a few stories where history comes alive through individual people. Also from Good News Network, diaries written during the Second World War have revealed the bravery of Ada Le Poidevin, a shopkeeper on Guernsey. She hid three British soldiers who had been left behind after a raid, keeping them from the Nazis. Her courage only came to light forty years after her death. It reads like a novel, and it teaches the occupation of the Channel Islands through one quiet, determined woman behind a shop counter.

Good News Network has another wartime tale, a gentler one. Rodney Anderson, an eighty-one-year-old Englishman, has found his long-lost Canadian relatives with the help of a family-tree search. A wartime encounter had divided the two families for eight decades, and now they are united. It is a moving reminder that history is often a matter of who went missing from whose life, and that sometimes, at last, they are found.

And from Upworthy comes a link across time in writing. Gertrude Bustill Mossell launched a column in eighteen eighty-five dedicated to the achievements and struggles of Black women. The piece connects her work to the writing career of the character Peggy Scott on The Gilded Age, suggesting that the fiction echoes a real journalist who made her own rules. The article is brief, but it is a neat example of a television drama pointing back to a true and rather inspiring history.

Now some stories of kindness and community. Upworthy tells us about Brian Schwartz, who lost his job and began mowing lawns for free. His gesture has grown into a nationwide network of around two thousand one hundred volunteers, connecting neighbours with practical help. It is a very concrete sort of generosity, the kind you can see out of a window.

Also from Upworthy, Josh Staub, the animator who worked on Frozen, has launched an interactive app for learning American Sign Language. He made it as a labour of love with Deaf animators, engineers and other collaborators, and has pledged to keep it free forever. It is a good example of education and access going hand in hand, and of a community building something for itself.

And one more from Upworthy, which I confess I found properly moving. Brooklyn Dotson received a liver transplant as a baby, from a ten-year-old boy. This September she married his younger brother, Noah Waters. A donation that saved a life has, years later, become a family bond, which is the sort of plot a novelist might hesitate to invent.

Finally, a piece of good news for the planet. Good News Network reports that scientists believe a few remote coral atolls in the Pacific, teeming with life, may be among the last wild and healthy ecosystems untouched by humans. Two of them have now been declared sanctuaries. It is a concrete outcome rather than a promise, and a heartening thought that some places remain wholly themselves.

So, from a hidden self-portrait to a free sign-language app, I hope something here travels with you through the day, perhaps with a cup of tea and a view of Belledonne.

Good morning, Yamuna. It has been a rich couple of days for good news, with a lot of it coming from the world of books, paintings and old papers, and a little from the woods, the lawns and the coral reefs too.

Let me begin with the story that has filled the literary pages. M John Harrison has won the twenty twenty-six Booker Prize for fiction with a novel called The End of Everything. He is eighty-one, and NPR reports that he is the first science fiction author ever to win the prize. That is a real milestone for a genre that has so often been kept at the margins of literary prizes, whatever the quality of the writing inside it. The Guardian, in an editorial, calls the win a new frontier for science fiction, and it sets the novel within the longer history and development of the genre, so that the prize reads less like a one-off surprise and more like a moment when something long in the making has been acknowledged.

What I enjoyed most, though, were the two interviews, because they let you hear the man himself. The i Paper has him in wonderfully blunt form. His headline line is, "I'm going to die soon. I can do what I like." There is something very freeing in that, and very characterful: a writer who has spent a long career working, and is now, with a Booker in hand, declining to be solemn about it. The Irish Times gives us the other side of the same coin, a gentler and more private one. He says he is awake most of the night thinking, "This is extraordinary." I rather like the pairing. On one side, the dry, unsentimental voice; on the other, a man of eighty-one lying in the dark and not quite believing his luck. Late recognition can be bitter for some writers, but here it sounds like pure astonished delight. If you ever wanted a way to talk to your older pupils about what it means for a writer to be read, and to be recognised, these two pieces would make a lovely pair of texts to put side by side.

Staying with the world of stories and where they come from, The Borderlens reports on the Shillong Literary Fest, in north-east India, which brings together Khasi heritage and Booker laureates in a celebration of storytelling. I find that combination appealing. Oral tradition and local history sit alongside internationally famous prize-winners, and the festival treats them as part of the same conversation rather than as high and low. It is the sort of gathering where one can imagine stepping into a story without needing to know the culture first, which I know is something you value in fiction.

Now to paintings, and the pleasure of seeing how a great work was made. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that during the cleaning of Michelangelo's Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel, conservators have found an unprecedented technique and a hidden self-portrait by the artist. I should be honest that what we have is a short teaser, and the details of the technique and where the portrait is hidden are not yet in my notes. But the idea alone is wonderful: after all these centuries, with some of the most studied surface in Western art, there is still something concealed in it, and a patient cleaning has brought it into view. Michelangelo was also a poet, and I like the thought of him slipping his own face into the scene, a signature that is not quite a signature.

That idea of seeing a famous work in the making has a twin in the second story of this kind. Good News Network reports that a handwritten draft of Martin Luther King Junior's "I Have a Dream" speech has emerged from a desk drawer after six decades. It was written on the morning of the march to the Lincoln Memorial, and it is heavily revised. That is the detail I find most moving. We tend to meet that speech as a finished, almost musical piece of oratory, and here is the evidence of the crossings-out, the second thoughts, the care with which each phrase was weighed. For a teacher of literature, it is a gift: proof that rhythm and eloquence are worked for, and a page that students could look at to understand revision as part of the art rather than a sign of failure.

From drafts to diaries. Good News Network also carries a true wartime story that reads like a novel. Diaries from the Second World War reveal that Ada Le Poidevin, a shopkeeper on Guernsey, hid three British soldiers from the Nazis. The men had been left behind after a raid, and she sheltered them under the occupation. What makes it extraordinary is not only the courage but the silence. Her bravery came to light forty years after her death, through her own writing. There is something about the ordinariness of the figure, a woman who kept a shop, that makes the history close and personal in the way a good novel does. It is the kind of single life through which a whole period becomes understandable, and I can imagine it sitting beside a wartime novel on a first-year reading list.

A second story with a wartime beginning has a gentler ending. Good News Network reports that Rodney Anderson, an Englishman of eighty-one, has found his long-lost Canadian relatives with the help of a family-tree search. A wartime encounter had divided the two families for eight decades, and now it has united them. I love that the mystery was solved the modern way, through patient genealogy, and that it has given a man in his eighties a whole branch of family he did not know how to reach. It is a reminder that old stories are never entirely closed, and that somewhere a thread is waiting to be picked up.

There is a third piece which links history and writing, from Upworthy. It tells of Gertrude Bustill Mossell, who in eighteen eighty-five launched a newspaper column dedicated to the achievements and struggles of Black women. The article draws a line from her to Peggy Scott, the journalist character on The Gilded Age, whose writing career echoes hers. The piece itself is short, but the idea is a good one. A historical drama invents a character, and behind her stands a real woman who made her own rules, writing the column because nobody else was going to. It is a neat example of fiction pointing back towards the truth, and you may find it useful if you ever want pupils to ask what a novel or a television drama borrows from real lives.

Let me turn now to kindness, which this week has arrived in several sizes. The first is the most practical. Upworthy tells the story of Brian Schwartz, who lost his job and started mowing lawns for free. Now around two thousand one hundred volunteers have joined him, in a nationwide network that connects neighbours with practical help. I like how modest the beginning is: not a grand plan, just a man with a mower and some time on his hands, deciding that being out of work did not mean being of no use. And what grew from it is not a charity in the abstract but a very concrete set of neighbours helping neighbours. It made me think of the village life you have above the Grésivaudan, where a good deal of the real work of community happens through small, unremarkable gestures.

The second is a story of a different order, also from Upworthy, and I found it genuinely moving. Brooklyn Dotson received a liver transplant as a baby, and the donor was a ten-year-old boy. That child's liver saved her life. In September she married his younger brother, Noah Waters. The piece does not need embroidery. A gift made in the saddest of circumstances became, years later, a family bond and a wedding. If a novelist had invented it, one might have thought it too neat, and yet it is simply what happened.

The third is about access and education. Josh Staub, the animator who worked on Frozen, has launched an interactive app for learning American Sign Language. He made it as a labour of love, working with Deaf animators, engineers and other collaborators, and he has pledged to keep it free forever. I appreciate two things here. The first is that Deaf people helped to build it rather than simply being served by it. The second is the promise that it will stay free, which means the learning is open to anyone who wants it. For a teacher, there is something quietly inspiring in a tool that treats language as something to be shared rather than guarded.

And finally, something for the wider world. Good News Network reports that scientists have found a few remote coral atolls in the Pacific, teeming with life, that may be among the last wild and healthy ecosystems untouched by humans. Two of them have now been declared sanctuaries. What I like about this story is that it comes with an outcome rather than a hope: the protection has actually been put in place. There is a certain poetry in the idea of places still wholly themselves, with no human hand on them, and now guarded so they might stay that way. After a news cycle that so often speaks of loss, it is a relief to read about somewhere that has been kept.

If I step back, the stories seem to share a theme this week, which is things being found or revealed: a self-portrait under centuries of grime, a speech in a drawer, a diary that outlived its writer, a family on the other side of an ocean, a late and unexpected prize. Even the kinder stories have the same shape, of something small turning out to carry far more than anyone guessed. It is a good pattern to notice, and I think a rather literary one.

That is all for today, Yamuna, and I hope something here makes its way into a lesson, a walk or a good cup of tea in Les Adrets.

The report I have is brief, but that's the headline. In an interview with The Times of India, Harrison says fiction is a vibe, and that the novelist is a bit like T. S. Eliot: the job, he says, is to give people a feeling of something. It's a lovely line to carry into a classroom, a reminder that atmosphere and music in prose can matter as much as plot. If you'd like to hear how the evening unfolded, BBC Radio 4's Front Row has a thirty-minute special, recorded at Old Billingsgate in London. The shortlist of six included novels by Elizabeth Strout and Douglas Stuart, and the judges included Mary Beard and Jarvis Cocker.

Also out today is Stations, by Louise Kennedy, reviewed in The New York Times. It follows a young Irishwoman in London who tests the limits of commitment. It's a character-driven novel, and I suspect it's very much your sort of thing.

Now for some good news, starting with a story that could be a novel. Diaries have revealed the bravery of Ada Le Poidevin, a shopkeeper on Guernsey during the Second World War. After a raid, three British soldiers were left behind, and she hid them from the Nazis. Her courage only came to light forty years after her death, thanks to those diaries. It's history seen through a single, quietly remarkable person. From Good News Network, there's also something to lift the spirits from far away: scientists say a few remote coral atolls in the Pacific, teeming with life, may be among the last wild and healthy ecosystems untouched by humans, and two of them have now been declared sanctuaries.

For your viewing this week, ARTE has plenty. There's a documentary series called 1942, un monde en guerre, told through the voices of ordinary civilians across the world in the year the war became global. Episodes four to six are available until the eighth of May, twenty twenty-seven. That many-voiced approach has something of the novel about it. Also on ARTE, a film called Une vie pour l'art, about Gustave Fayet, who lived from eighteen sixty-five to nineteen twenty-five, an artist and a major collector of modern art. It accompanies an exhibition at the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris, and it threads together collecting, painting and modernity. And a more sobering title: a documentary on ARTE about the hundreds of thousands of Jews sold by communist Romania, reported by The Times of Israel. I only have the headline, but it's a weighty historical subject.

If you fancy a little opera, the Royal Opera has put Freddie De Tommaso singing Recondita armonia from Puccini's Tosca on YouTube. It's the aria that sets up the drama of Tosca, Cavaradossi and Scarpia, so it's a good three-minute way into the story.

Closer to home, there's something today. At two thirty this afternoon, the Musée de Grenoble offers a guided tour of the François Morellet exhibition, open to the public. The title is Sous la géométrie, la facétie, which promises playfulness beneath the geometry, and that sounds like a gentle way to spend a Sunday afternoon, if you can get down to the valley. Also in Grenoble, until the thirty-first of December, there's a free display on the military high-mountain group, the Groupe militaire de haute montagne. The details are slim, but it's a bit of local mountain history open for the rest of the year. And looking ahead, from the ninth to the eleventh of December, the MC2 stages Article 353 du code pénal, by Tanguy Viel and Emmanuel Noblet. It brings a literary text from Viel to the stage, so it might appeal if you enjoy fiction in performance.

A couple of items for your BFI corner. The BBC asks how Kent may have inspired Orwell's Animal Farm. I only have the headline, but it's a tempting thread, a novel tied to a real place. And the London Evening Standard has a feature on how Shakespeare and Radiohead came together to create a theatrical work, linking Hamlet with contemporary music. It could be a useful angle on adaptation.

Finally, two items from France. Franceinfo reports that Michel Destot, mayor of Grenoble from nineteen ninety-five to twenty fourteen and member of parliament for the third constituency of the Isère, died yesterday at the age of eighty. His name will be familiar to anyone who lives around the city. And franceinfo also recommends Aya, pour l'exemple, a hybrid essay by the critic Christelle Bakima-Poundza on Aya Nakamura and the cultures that opened the way for her in France. It's presented as a portrait of a France with unlimited dreams, and a fine example of culture set against a wider social picture.

That's all for this morning, Yamuna. I hope your Sunday is full of good reading and good light over Belledonne.
